evidence: The OrderService constructor takes domain ports (OrderRepository, ProductRepository, IdGenerator, Clock) instead of concrete persistence classes.

placeOrder hands the stock rules to product.canReserve and product.reserve, and builds the order with new Order(...). It only coordinates the work across aggregates and saves through the repositories.
changeState and cancel hand state rules to order.transitionTo and stock changes to product.ship and product.release.
The file contains no HTTP, framework, SQL or storage code.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: src/application/order-service.ts is an application service doing use-case orchestration. It works only through domain ports that are injected into it: OrderRepository, ProductRepository, IdGenerator and Clock. It has no persistence code (no SQL, file I/O or database clients), no transport code (no HTTP request or response handling) and no framework code. The core business rules stay in domain objects: Product.canReserve/reserve/ship/release, Order.transitionTo/nextState and assertPositiveInteger. The service coordinates work that spans more than one aggregate. It reserves stock for the whole order or none of it, ships stock when an order is shipped, and releases stock when an order is cancelled. That cross-aggregate coordination is a normal application-layer job. Two small checks could arguably live in the Order aggregate: the empty-items check in placeOrder and the merging of duplicate product lines into one quantity. Both are input validation at the use-case boundary rather than misplaced responsibilities, so they don't fail the rubric.
